name: The Domino Theory
statement: Let one country fall to an ideology and its neighbours topple in turn, like a row of dominoes.
meaning: The domino theory was a Cold War doctrine holding that a political event in one country, above all the fall of a state to communism, would trigger the fall of its neighbours in a chain reaction, each collapse knocking over the next like a row of standing dominoes. It framed the loss of even a small or peripheral country as intolerable, because the danger lay not in that country alone but in the cascade it was expected to set off across a whole region. The image made containment feel urgent everywhere at once: no falling piece could be written off as local.
mechanism: The theory rests on a contagion metaphor. A communist takeover was imagined to spread by demonstration effect, subversion, and the material and moral support a new communist state would give insurgents next door, so that each fall raised the odds and lowered the cost of the next. Because the dominoes were assumed to be tightly coupled, the model implied that the chain had to be broken early and far forward, justifying intervention in distant countries of little intrinsic value to prevent a regional collapse. Its persuasive force came almost entirely from the vividness of the falling-dominoes picture rather than from any demonstrated mechanism of transmission.

examples.text: At an April 1954 press conference, President Eisenhower described a row of dominoes: knock over the first and the last will fall quickly, invoked to explain why Indochina mattered to the wider region.
The theory became a central justification for deepening US military involvement in Vietnam, on the reasoning that a communist South Vietnam would topple the rest of Southeast Asia.

After Saigon fell in 1975, Laos and Cambodia did go communist, a limited local toppling, but the predicted region-wide collapse of Thailand, Indonesia, and beyond did not occur, and several of those states grew stronger.

variants.name: The containment antecedent
variants.text: The idea predates the name: the reasoning behind the 1947 Truman Doctrine, that abandoning Greece and Turkey would let communism spread onward, is the same logic without the domino image.

variants.name: Lee Kuan Yew's partial defence
variants.text: Singapore's Lee Kuan Yew argued the theory was not simply wrong, contending that US intervention in Vietnam, however costly, bought time that let the non-communist states of ASEAN stabilise and develop.

whyItMatters: The domino theory was one of the most consequential foreign-policy ideas of the twentieth century, shaping US strategy across four administrations and helping justify the Vietnam War and interventions elsewhere. As a case study it is a cautionary tale about how a vivid metaphor can substitute for analysis, flattening diverse countries into interchangeable pieces and treating a contested empirical claim as self-evident. It remains a live reference in debates over credibility, chain-reaction thinking, and whether standing firm in one place is needed to hold the line everywhere.

working.text: recognise the argument that one loss mechanically causes the next, so a peripheral place must be held to prevent a regional collapse.
ask whether the pieces are really tightly linked, since countries have distinct histories, nationalisms, and interests that resist any uniform cascade.
treat the seductive falling-dominoes image as a reason for extra scrutiny, not proof, since metaphor is not mechanism.

limits: The theory is largely discredited as a general law. Its central prediction failed the crucial test: after South Vietnam fell in 1975, the wider region did not collapse, and Southeast Asia's non-communist states endured and prospered, though Laos and Cambodia did fall, a limited local confirmation rather than the sweeping cascade forecast. Critics fault it for treating varied nations as identical, interchangeable pieces, for ignoring the fierce nationalism that set communist states against one another, as with China and Vietnam, and for mistaking a metaphor for a causal model. Defenders such as Lee Kuan Yew argue it captured a real, if narrower, dynamic and that intervention bought decisive time, so its status is contested rather than wholly dismissed.
misreadings: The theory did not originate with Eisenhower; he supplied the memorable name and image in 1954, but the underlying containment logic was already explicit in the 1947 Truman Doctrine. It is not a validated law: its headline prediction of a region-wide collapse after 1975 did not come to pass. It is not entirely baseless either, since Laos and Cambodia did fall and defenders argue intervention bought time, so the honest verdict is a largely failed but still-debated theory rather than a simple hoax. And it is a claim about political chain reactions, not the unrelated everyday sense of a domino effect in mechanics or accidents.
origin: The falling-domino image was popularised by US President Dwight D. Eisenhower at an April 7, 1954 press conference on Indochina, though the containment reasoning behind it dates to the early Cold War and the 1947 Truman Doctrine.
